newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Hungary is darling of foreign direct investors.
newsitem.headline: Hungary is darling of foreign direct investors.

text.p: Hungary ranked number one in foreign direct investment to the former communist world as of mid-1996 with a cumulative $13.9 billion, followed by Poland with $9.1 billion, a new U.N. report said on Tuesday.

Figures released by the U.N. Economic Commission for Europe (ECE), a specialised United Nations agency for economic cooperation in Europe, showed countries that reformed faster enjoyed the biggest share of foreign direct investment.
Foreign direct investment to the transitional economies topped more than $46 billion as of mid-1996, up 60 percent over a year ago, the ECE said.

Hungary accounted for 30 percent of total foreign direct investments in the ex-communist world, followed by Poland with a 17-percent share. Russia came third with a 13-percent share, beating the Czech republic to fourth place with 12 percent.

Overall, Hungary, the Czech Republic, Poland, the Slovak Republic and Slovenia accounted for nearly 70 percent of the total foreign direct investment to the former communist countries as of mid-1996, the ECE said.

Although tiny by Western standards, the per capita share of foreign direct investment in transitional economies more than doubled to $135 at the start of 1996 from $60 at the start of 1994, the report said.
This is way below some $1,800 in per capita foreign direct investment in the United States but is more than Brazil's $130 and some $110 in China, it said.
At the bottom of the league, per capita foreign investment in Ukraine was only $17 and $20 in Moldova.
